profile.feeling: The plain “I” — often left out, because the verb already says who is speaking.

senses.def: the ego, the self (as a noun: الْأَنَا)

examples.tr: I am a student — and you?

examples.text: أَنَا أُحِبُّ الْقَهْوَةَ، أَمَّا هُوَ فَيُحِبُّ الشَّايَ.
examples.tr: I like coffee, whereas he likes tea.
The book talks about the self and the other.

profile.synonymsNone: No other independent “I”; as object or possessor Arabic uses the suffixes ـنِي / ـي (forms, not synonyms).

etymology.text: Inherited from Proto-Semitic *ʔanāku; cognate with Hebrew אֲנִי (aní) and Amharic እኔ (enē); compare Egyptian jnk (Coptic ⲁⲛⲟⲕ, anok).

funFacts: The noun الْأَنَا, “the ego”, is a semantic loan from German “das Ich” (Wiktionary).
pitfalls: Written with a final alif, but in connected MSA speech the last vowel is short: ʾana. The alif is pronounced long only at a pause.
The pronoun is not needed with a verb: آكُلُ alone already means “I eat”.
subtleties: أَنَا before a verb adds emphasis or contrast: أَنَا آكُلُ = it is I who eat (not someone else).

profile.feeling: Direct and everyday — used even with strangers; politeness comes from titles, not from the pronoun.

senses.def: you (one man; masculine singular subject pronoun)

examples.tr: You are my friend. (to a man)
Where are you from? (to a man)

synonyms.nuance: lit. “your presence” — a polite way to address a man, very common in Egypt; grammatically a noun with a suffix, not a pronoun

etymology.text: Inherited from Proto-Semitic *ʔanta (Wiktionary); Hebrew אַתָּה (atá) continues the same form with the n assimilated.

funFacts: The -ta of أَنْتَ is the same ending as in the past verb: كَتَبْتَ, “you (m.) wrote”.
pitfalls: أَنْتَ (man) and أَنْتِ (woman) are the same letters, انت; only the final vowel differs (-ta / -ti). In unvocalized text only the context tells you.
With أَنْتَ the present verb starts with تَـ and has no ending: أَنْتَ تَأْكُلُ — the same form as “she eats” (هِيَ تَأْكُلُ).
subtleties: Arabic has no built-in polite “you” like German Sie or Russian вы: respect is shown with titles and formulas (حَضْرَتُكَ, يَا أُسْتَاذُ).

profile.feeling: The same everyday “you”, addressed to one woman.

senses.def: you (one woman; feminine singular subject pronoun)

examples.tr: You are my friend. (to a woman)
Where are you from? (to a woman)

synonyms.nuance: lit. “your presence” — polite address to a woman, very common in Egypt; a noun with a suffix, not a pronoun

etymology.text: Inherited from Proto-Semitic *ʔanti (Wiktionary); compare the Hebrew feminine אַתְּ (at).

funFacts: Hebrew lost the n in אַתְּ (at); Arabic keeps it: ʾanti.
pitfalls: The verb after أَنْتِ ends in -īna: أَنْتِ تَأْكُلِينَ, تَشْرَبِينَ — not تَأْكُلُ.
Same letters as أَنْتَ (انت): only the kasra (-ti) shows that a woman is meant.
subtleties: Adjectives agree too: أَنْتِ جَاهِزَةٌ (to a woman) vs أَنْتَ جَاهِزٌ (to a man).

profile.feeling: Neutral; also “it” for every masculine thing.

senses.def: he (third person masculine singular subject pronoun)
it (referring to a masculine noun, also a thing)

examples.tr: The book? It is on the table.

profile.synonymsNone: No synonym: هُوَ is the only third-person masculine singular subject pronoun (as object or possessor: the suffix ـهُ).

etymology.text: Inherited from Proto-Semitic *šuʔa (Wiktionary); compare Hebrew הוּא (hu).

funFacts: Psychology’s “id” is الْهُوَ in Arabic — a calque of Freud’s German “Es” (Wiktionary), just as الْأَنَا is “das Ich”.
pitfalls: هُوَ also means “it” for masculine nouns: الْبَصَلُ؟ هُوَ هُنَا = the onions? They (lit. it) are here. Do not always translate “he”.
subtleties: Between a subject and a definite predicate, هُوَ / هِيَ can act like a copula (ḍamīr al-faṣl): الْمُشْكِلَةُ هِيَ الْوَقْتُ = the problem is time.

profile.feeling: Neutral; also “it” for feminine things — and “they” for non-human plurals.

senses.def: she (third person feminine singular subject pronoun)

examples.tr: The car? It is in front of the house.
The books? They are on the table.

profile.synonymsNone: No synonym: هِيَ is the only third-person feminine singular subject pronoun (as object or possessor: the suffix ـهَا).

etymology.text: Inherited from Proto-Semitic *šiʔa (Wiktionary); compare Hebrew הִיא (hi).

funFacts: Hebrew הִיא (hi) is the same Semitic word.
pitfalls: Non-human plurals are referred to with هِيَ, not هُمْ: الْجَزَرَاتُ؟ هِيَ هُنَا = the carrots? They are here.
subtleties: The verb after هِيَ starts with تَـ, like the verb after أَنْتَ: هِيَ تَأْكُلُ / أَنْتَ تَأْكُلُ.

profile.feeling: Togetherness: family, team, “us”.

senses.def: we (first person plural subject pronoun; also for two people)

profile.synonymsNone: No synonym: نَحْنُ is the only first-person plural subject pronoun (as object or possessor: the suffix ـنَا).

etymology.text: Inherited from Proto-Semitic *niḥnu; cognate with Hebrew אֲנַחְנוּ (anáchnu).

funFacts: The same n appears in the suffix “us/our”: بَيْتُنَا (our house), عِنْدَنَا (we have).
pitfalls: The final -u is fixed: نَحْنُ never changes with case.
The present verb with نَحْنُ starts with نَـ: نَأْكُلُ، نَشْرَبُ، نُحِبُّ.
subtleties: Used for men, women and mixed groups, and also for two people: Arabic has no dual “we”.

profile.feeling: A group of people — men, or men and women together.
profile.synonymsNone: No synonym: هُنَّ is its feminine counterpart (only women), and هُمَا is for exactly two.

etymology.text: Inherited from Proto-Semitic *šum (Wiktionary); compare Hebrew הֵם (hem).

funFacts: For exactly two people Arabic uses the dual هُمَا — a living dual that Hebrew pronouns no longer have.
pitfalls: A mixed group takes هُمْ: one man among women is enough for the masculine.
Not for things: non-human plurals are هِيَ (الْبَصَلَاتُ؟ هِيَ هُنَا).
subtleties: When هُمْ comes first, the verb agrees fully (هُمْ يَأْكُلُونَ); a noun subject after the verb leaves the verb singular (يَأْكُلُ الطُّلَّابُ).

profile.feeling: A group of women only.

senses.def: they (feminine plural, a group of women)

profile.synonymsNone: No synonym: هُمْ is the masculine/mixed counterpart.

etymology.text: Feminine plural of the inherited Semitic third-person pronoun series (هُوَ، هِيَ، هُمْ، هُنَّ); Hebrew הֵן (hen) is the corresponding form.
etymology.src: Arabic and Hebrew grammars (Wiktionary has no etymology for this entry)

funFacts: The double n (šadda) is what distinguishes هُنَّ (they, f.) from هُنَا (here).
pitfalls: The verb after هُنَّ ends in -na: هُنَّ يَأْكُلْنَ، يَشْرَبْنَ — the 2nd person “you (women)” has the same ending: تَأْكُلْنَ.
Only for a group made up entirely of women; one man in the group → هُمْ.
subtleties: Most spoken dialects have lost the feminine plural and say هُمْ for women too; Modern Standard Arabic requires هُنَّ.

profile.feeling: The invisible verb: absent in the present, essential for past and future.

senses.def: to be (past and future; the present “is” is not expressed)
auxiliary: كَانَ + present verb = past continuous or habit (“was doing, used to do”)
to exist, to be; there was (Wiktionary: “to exist, to be, there be”)

examples.tr: I will be at home tomorrow.
She was eating when I arrived.

examples.text: كَانَ يَا مَا كَانَ، فِي قَدِيمِ الزَّمَانِ…
examples.tr: Once upon a time, long, long ago…

collocations.tr: I had (lit. there was at me)

phrases.text: كَانَ يَا مَا كَانَ، فِي قَدِيمِ الزَّمَانِ
phrases.tr: there was, or there was not, in the old days
phrases.meaning: the traditional opening of a fairy tale: once upon a time

profile.synonymsNone: No real synonym. Its “sisters” (أَخَوَاتُ كَانَ: أَصْبَحَ “to become”, صَارَ “to become”, ظَلَّ “to remain”, لَيْسَ “not to be”) work the same way but add a meaning.

etymology.text: From Proto-Semitic *kawan- (“to be or exist in a place”); root ك و ن, verbal noun كَوْن (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Arab fairy tales start with كَانَ يَا مَا كَانَ — “once upon a time”.
The same root gives مَكَان (place) and كَوْن (being; the universe).
pitfalls: No verb “to be” in the present: هُوَ طَبِيبٌ = he is a doctor. Never *هُوَ يَكُونُ طَبِيبٌ for a simple “is”.
Its predicate is accusative: الْجَوُّ جَمِيلٌ → كَانَ الْجَوُّ جَمِيلًا.
Hollow verb: the long ā shortens before consonant endings — كَانَ but كُنْتُ (I was), كُنَّا (we were).
subtleties: The present forms (يَكُونُ …) do exist: for the future (سَيَكُونُ), for habits and general truths, and after أَنْ (يَجِبُ أَنْ يَكُونَ = he must be).

profile.feeling: Basic and everyday; in figurative use, something that slowly destroys.

senses.def: to eat away, corrode, consume (rust, fire, time)

examples.tr: What do you eat for breakfast?

phrases.tr: time has eaten and drunk on it
phrases.meaning: it is very old, worn out or outdated

synonyms.nuance: to have, take (a meal, medicine) — news, menus and polite speech
to devour, gobble up

etymology.text: From Proto-Semitic *ʔakal-; cognate with Hebrew אָכַל (akhal) and Aramaic ʾăḵal.

funFacts: The imperative is just كُلْ (kul, ‘eat!’): like خُذْ (‘take!’) and مُرْ (‘order!’) it drops its first radical, the hamza.
pitfalls: I eat = آكُلُ (ʾākulu): hamza + long ā is written with madda, آ.
The vowel of the 2nd radical changes: a in the past (أَكَلَ), u in the present (يَأْكُلُ).
subtleties: In formal Arabic, especially for meals, تَنَاوَلَ is preferred: تَنَاوَلْنَا الْغَدَاءَ (we had lunch).

profile.feeling: Everyday and social: tea, coffee, hospitality.

examples.tr: What will you (f) have to drink?
My grandfather smokes shisha at the café.

phrases.meaning: do what you like, I don’t care (a rude dismissal)

synonyms.nuance: to have, take (food, drink, medicine) — polite and written style
to sip, drink slowly (a hot drink)

etymology.text: Root ش ر ب; compare Akkadian sarāpum (“to suck”) and Geʿez ሠረበ (śäräbä).

funFacts: English syrup and sherbet, Turkish şerbet and Greek σιρόπι all come from this root: شَرَاب / شَرْبَة, “a drink”.
pitfalls: The vowel changes: šariba (past, i) → yašrabu (present, a). Not *yašribu.
شَرَّبَ with šadda is a different verb: “to make drink, to soak” (form II).
subtleties: In formal or polite language تَنَاوَلَ is preferred for meals and medicine: تَنَاوَلَ الدَّوَاءَ.

profile.feeling: Markets, shopping, bargaining.

examples.tr: I bought bread at the bakery.
What are you buying for dinner?

examples.text: نَشْتَرِي الْخُضَارَ مِنَ السُّوقِ كُلَّ أُسْبُوعٍ.
examples.tr: We buy vegetables at the market every week.
My sister bought a new dress.

synonyms.nuance: to buy, purchase — written and formal style
classical form I: can mean “to buy” but also “to sell” (Wiktionary)

etymology.text: Form VIII (pattern اِفْتَعَلَ) of the root ش ر ي, whose form I شَرَى can mean both “to sell” and “to buy” (Wiktionary).

funFacts: مُشْتَرٍ means “buyer” — and الْمُشْتَرِي is also the planet Jupiter.
pitfalls: Weak final radical: the y appears as -ā, -ī or -ay — اِشْتَرَى (he bought), يَشْتَرِي (he buys), اِشْتَرَيْتُ (I bought), اِشْتَرَوْا (they bought).
تَشْتَرِينَ is both “you (one woman) buy” and “you (women) buy”.
subtleties: The initial alif is a connecting hamza (hamzat al-waṣl): after a vowel it is silent — وَاشْتَرَى (wa-štarā).

profile.feeling: Warm; from “I like onions” to “I love you”.

examples.tr: Do you like tea with mint?

collocations.tr: to love with all one’s heart

phrases.text: مَنْ أَحَبَّ شَيْئًا أَكْثَرَ مِنْ ذِكْرِهِ
phrases.tr: whoever loves a thing mentions it often
phrases.meaning: people keep talking about what they love

synonyms.nuance: to love passionately, be infatuated
to love, be fond of — classical and poetic
“to please”: أَعْجَبَنِي الْفِيلْمُ = I liked the film — the thing liked is the subject

etymology.text: Form IV of the root ح ب ب; the verbal nouns are حُبّ (love) and مَحَبَّة (affection) (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Turkish muhabbet (friendly chat, affection) comes from Arabic مَحَبَّة, from the same root; Hebrew חִבָּה (ḥiba, fondness) is a Semitic cousin.
pitfalls: Form IV: the present has u-prefixes — أُحِبُّ (ʾuḥibbu), يُحِبُّ — not *أَحِبُّ.
Doubled root: before a consonant ending the two b’s come apart — أَحْبَبْتُ (I loved), يُحْبِبْنَ (they, women, love).
subtleties: أُحِبُّ means both “I like” and “I love”; the object decides: أُحِبُّ الْبَصَلَ (I like onions) vs أُحِبُّكِ (I love you).
To like doing: أُحِبُّ + verbal noun (أُحِبُّ السِّبَاحَةَ) or أَنْ + subjunctive (أُحِبُّ أَنْ أَسْبَحَ).

profile.feeling: Wishes and intentions; direct, so softened with مِنْ فَضْلِكَ.

examples.text: أُرِيدُ كُوبًا مِنَ الْمَاءِ، مِنْ فَضْلِكَ.
examples.tr: I would like a glass of water, please.
What do you (f) want to eat?
They want to travel to Morocco.

examples.text: فَوَجَدَا فِيهَا جِدَارًا يُرِيدُ أَنْ يَنْقَضَّ
examples.tr: and they found in it a wall about to collapse (Qurʾān 18:77)

phrases.text: إِذَا أَرَدْتَ أَنْ تُطَاعَ فَأْمُرْ بِمَا يُسْتَطَاعُ
phrases.tr: if you want to be obeyed, order what can be done
phrases.meaning: make demands that people are able to meet

synonyms.nuance: to wish, would like — very polite: أَوَدُّ أَنْ أَشْكُرَكُمْ (I would like to thank you)
to desire, wish for — written and official style

etymology.text: Form IV of the root ر و د; verbal noun إِرَادَة, “will, intention” (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Turkish irade (will, decree) and mürit (disciple) come from Arabic إِرَادَة and مُرِيد, “one who wants”, from this root.
pitfalls: Hollow verb: the long ī/ā shortens before consonant endings — تُرِيدُ but تُرِدْنَ (you, women, want); أَرَادَ but أَرَدْتُ (I wanted).
Form IV: present with u-prefix — أُرِيدُ, يُرِيدُ (not *أَرِيدُ).
subtleties: Followed by a noun (أُرِيدُ خُبْزًا) or by أَنْ + subjunctive (أُرِيدُ أَنْ آكُلَ). In a shop, أُرِيدُ + مِنْ فَضْلِكَ is fine; أَوَدُّ is more formal.

profile.feeling: The “is not” of Arabic: a whole verb that only negates.

senses.def: is not, am not, are not — negates a sentence without a verb (present)

phrases.meaning: seeing for yourself is better than any report

synonyms.nuance: “non-, un-, other than” before a noun or adjective: غَيْرُ صَحِيحٍ = incorrect (a noun, not a verb)
negates a nominal sentence in classical style: مَا هٰذَا بَشَرًا (Qurʾān 12:31, “this is not a human being”)

etymology.text: Uncertain (Wiktionary): traditionally explained as a contraction of لَا “not” + an old existential أَيْس “there is”, which would be cognate with Hebrew יֵשׁ (yesh, “there is”) — or of an unexplained verb لَيِسَ.

funFacts: Arabic has no verb for “is” in the present — but it has one for “is not”.
pitfalls: Its predicate is accusative: هُوَ طَبِيبٌ → لَيْسَ طَبِيبًا.
It looks like a past verb (لَيْسَ، لَسْتُ، لَيْسُوا) but means the present: لَسْتُ جَائِعًا = I am not hungry.
To negate a present verb use لَا, not لَيْسَ: لَا أُحِبُّ (I don’t like).
subtleties: The stem shortens to las- before consonant endings: لَيْسَ but لَسْتُ، لَسْنَا، لَسْنَ.
It agrees with its subject: هٰذِهِ لَيْسَتْ جَزَرَةً (feminine), هٰذَا لَيْسَ بَصَلًا (masculine).

profile.feeling: The everyday “have”: literally “at me, at you” — possession as location.

senses.def: to have — عِنْدَ + pronoun suffix: عِنْدِي “at me” = I have
at, near, with, at the house of

examples.tr: She has a brother and two sisters.

synonyms.nuance: at, with; لَدَيَّ = I have — the written, formal counterpart of عِنْدِي
for, belonging to: لِي أَخٌ = I have a brother — for relatives, rights and lasting relations
with: مَعِي قَلَمٌ = I have a pen (on me, right now)

etymology.text: A contraction of ع ن ن or ع ي ن (in the sense of viewing) and يَدَا (“hand”), i.e. “at hand, before one’s eyes”; compare لَدَى and لَدُنْ.

funFacts: عِنْدَمَا (“when”) is simply عِنْدَ + مَا.
pitfalls: عِنْدَ is a preposition, not a verb: it does not change for tense. “I had” = كَانَ عِنْدِي; “I don’t have” = لَيْسَ عِنْدِي.
The thing you have is the grammatical subject, so it is nominative and usually indefinite: عِنْدِي جَزَرَةٌ (not جَزَرَةً).
Unvocalized عند can also be the verb عَنَدَ, “to be stubborn” (root of عِنَاد, stubbornness — Turkish inat).
subtleties: عِنْدِي is for what you own or keep at your place, لِي for relations and rights, مَعِي for what you carry right now.

profile.feeling: Clear and polite; as a question (نَعَمْ؟) it answers a call.

senses.def: yes? (answering when called; asking someone to go on)

examples.text: — هَلْ أَنْتَ جَاهِزٌ؟ — نَعَمْ، أَنَا جَاهِزٌ.

examples.tr: Yes, I’d like coffee without sugar.
He said yes to the offer.

synonyms.nuance: yes, indeed — more formal or literary
yes (on the contrary) — the answer that contradicts a negative question
everyday spoken “yes”

etymology.text: Wiktionary links it to the root ن ع م (“to be pleased, to live in comfort”), cognate with Hebrew נָעַם (naʿam, “to please”).

funFacts: Hebrew נָעִים (naʿim, “pleasant”) — as in נָעִים מְאוֹד, “nice to meet you” — comes from the same Semitic root.
pitfalls: To a negative question, “yes, it is so” is بَلَى, not نَعَمْ: أَلَيْسَ هٰذَا بَصَلًا؟ — بَلَى (Isn’t this onion? — Yes, it is). نَعَمْ would confirm the negative.
Unvocalized نعم can also be نِعْمَ (“how excellent …!”) or نَعَم (cattle) — the vowels and the final sukūn of نَعَمْ tell them apart.
subtleties: Said as a question, نَعَمْ؟ means “yes? / pardon?”; with a sharp tone it can sound like “excuse me?!”.

profile.feeling: A plain “no”; in hospitality, often said once and then overruled by the host.

phrases.tr: no, and a thousand times no

synonyms.nuance: no, by no means — an emphatic rejection, frequent in the Qurʾān
everyday spoken “no”

etymology.text: Inherited from Proto-Semitic *lā; compare Hebrew לֹא (lo).

funFacts: Hebrew לֹא (lo) is the same Proto-Semitic word *lā — and it also means both “no” and “not”.
pitfalls: The answer “no” and the negation “not” are the same written word لَا (separate words in this course). As an answer it stands alone, usually followed by a comma; as negation it stands directly before a present verb: لَا أُحِبُّ.
subtleties: A first لَا to food or drink is often not taken as final in Arab hospitality — the host may insist; a firm refusal usually repeats it with thanks: لَا، شُكْرًا.

profile.feeling: The workhorse negation of the present; also in many fixed phrases.

senses.def: there is no … (with a noun in -a without tanwīn)

examples.tr: There is no doubt about that.

phrases.text: لَا يُلْدَغُ الْمُؤْمِنُ مِنْ جُحْرٍ وَاحِدٍ مَرَّتَيْنِ
phrases.tr: a believer is not stung from the same hole twice
phrases.meaning: a wise person does not fall for the same trick twice (a hadith used as a proverb)

synonyms.nuance: negates a sentence without a verb (“is not”), conjugated
negates the past, with the jussive: لَمْ آكُلْ (I didn’t eat)
negates the future, with the subjunctive: لَنْ آكُلَ (I won’t eat)
negates a past verb (also very common in the dialects): مَا أَكَلْتُ

etymology.text: Inherited from Proto-Semitic *lā; compare Hebrew לֹא (lo).

funFacts: Modern Arabic uses لَا like a prefix “non-, un-”: لَاسِلْكِيّ (wireless, lit. “no-wire-ish”).
pitfalls: لَا negates the present only. Past: لَمْ + jussive (لَمْ آكُلْ); future: لَنْ + subjunctive (لَنْ آكُلَ).
Written exactly like the answer لَا “no” — read the position: before a verb it means “not”.
subtleties: The verb after لَا stays indicative: لَا أُحِبُّ (-u); after لَا of prohibition it is jussive: لَا تَقْلَقْ (-∅).
لَا + noun = “there is no”: لَا شَكَّ — the noun takes -a without tanwīn.

profile.feeling: Everywhere: Arabic links clauses with وَ far more than English uses “and”.

examples.tr: My brother and I are at home.

collocations.tr: and so on, and so forth

synonyms.nuance: and then, afterwards — sequence with a gap in time
and so, and then — immediate sequence or consequence

etymology.text: From Proto-Semitic *wa; cognate with Hebrew וְ־ (ve-).

funFacts: Hebrew וְ (ve-) is the same Semitic word and is also written joined to the next word.
pitfalls: وَ is never written alone: it joins the next word — وَالْبَصَلُ، وَأَنَا.
In lists Arabic repeats وَ before every item: جَزَرٌ وَبَصَلٌ وَثُومٌ.
subtleties: Before al- the connecting hamza is silent: وَالْبَصَلُ = wa-l-baṣalu.
Arabic prose often begins sentences with وَ; translating every one as “and” sounds odd in English.

profile.feeling: Pointing at what is near.

senses.def: this (near) — masculine هٰذَا, feminine هٰذِهِ, plural (people) هٰؤُلَاءِ

profile.synonymsNone: No synonym in MSA; هٰذِي is a rarer variant of the feminine (Wiktionary).

etymology.text: Univerbation of هَا (attention particle) + ذَا; cognate with Hebrew הַזֶּה (hazé, “this”).

funFacts: Hebrew הַזֶּה (hazé) and Arabic هٰذَا share the same deictic element: Arabic ذ = Hebrew ז.
pitfalls: The first ā is written with a small (dagger) alif, not a full one: هٰذَا. Unvocalized it is just هذا.
هٰذَا الْبَصَلُ = this onion (a phrase); هٰذَا بَصَلٌ = this is onion (a sentence). The article makes the difference.
subtleties: Non-human plurals take the feminine singular: هٰذِهِ جَزَرَاتٌ (these are carrots); هٰؤُلَاءِ is only for people.

profile.feeling: The question before a verb: what do you…?

synonyms.nuance: before nouns and pronouns: مَا هٰذَا؟ مَا اسْمُكَ؟
spoken “what”, after the verb
spoken “what”

etymology.text: From مَا (mā) + ذَا (ḏā).

funFacts: لِمَاذَا, “why”, is literally “for what”.
pitfalls: Use مَاذَا before a verb (مَاذَا تَشْرَبُ؟) but مَا before a noun or pronoun (مَا هٰذَا؟).
subtleties: Formal Arabic also uses مَاذَا before a past verb: مَاذَا فَعَلْتَ؟ (what did you do?).

profile.feeling: Short and frequent — and with many jobs.

synonyms.nuance: the form used before a verb: مَاذَا تَأْكُلُ؟

etymology.text: Cognate with Hebrew מָה (ma) and Ugaritic mh.

funFacts: Hebrew מָה (ma, “what”) is the same Semitic word.
pitfalls: مَا is also the negation “not” (مَا أَكَلْتُ = I didn’t eat) and the relative “what, that which” (أَعْرِفُ مَا تُرِيدُ = I know what you want). Only position and context tell them apart.
subtleties: In the exclamation مَا أَجْمَلَ …! the noun is accusative: مَا أَجْمَلَ الْبَحْرَ!

profile.feeling: Finding your way: places, people, things.

senses.def: where? (also مِنْ أَيْنَ “from where”, إِلَى أَيْنَ “where to”)
how can … compare with …? (أَيْنَ X مِنْ Y — implying there is no comparison)

examples.tr: Where are you from? (to a woman)
How can this even compare with that?

synonyms.nuance: spoken “where”
spoken “where”

etymology.text: From the root ء ي ن (“to come or approach”, “to draw near to a place or time”); related to آن (ʾān, “time, now”) (Wiktionary).

funFacts: The Qurʾān asks: فَأَيْنَ تَذْهَبُونَ؟ — “So where are you going?” (81:26).
pitfalls: No verb “is” after it: أَيْنَ الْمَحَطَّةُ؟ = where is the station? The noun is nominative.
أَيْنَ always ends in -a; it never takes case endings.
subtleties: أَيْنَمَا + jussive = “wherever”: أَيْنَمَا تَذْهَبْ أَذْهَبْ (wherever you go, I go).

profile.feeling: Presence: “here I am”, “here it is”.

senses.def: at this point, then, now (in a story or argument)

examples.text: مِنْ هُنَا إِلَى الْمَطَارِ عِشْرُونَ دَقِيقَةً.
examples.tr: It is twenty minutes from here to the airport.
And this is where the problem began.

synonyms.nuance: here — classical form
spoken “here”
spoken “here”

etymology.text: Compare Hebrew הִנֵּה (hinne, “here is, behold”) (Wiktionary).

funFacts: هُنَا الْقَاهِرَةُ — “Here is Cairo” — was the famous call sign of Egyptian state radio.
pitfalls: هُنَاكَ (there) is هُنَا + -ka, and it also means “there is / there are”: هُنَاكَ مُشْكِلَةٌ = there is a problem.
Do not confuse هُنَا (hunā, here) with هُنَّ (hunna, they — women).
subtleties: In a sentence without a verb هُنَا is the predicate: الْبَصَلُ هُنَا = the onions are here.

lexemes.role: Yes/no question particle: put it at the start of a statement to turn it into a question (هَلْ تُحِبُّ الْجَزَرَ؟).

profile.feeling: Neutral question marker of written Arabic.

senses.def: yes/no question marker (placed before the statement)

synonyms.nuance: prefix question marker (أَتُحِبُّ …؟); required before a negation: أَلَيْسَ …؟

etymology.text: Univerbation of هَـ (ha-, an old interrogative, now أَ) + لـ (l-, an affirmative particle) (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Word order never changes in an Arabic question — هَلْ is all you add.
pitfalls: Before al- it takes a helping vowel: هَلِ الْبَصَلُ طَازَجٌ؟ (not هَلْ الْ…).
Not before a negation: “don’t you like …?” = أَلَا تُحِبُّ …؟ (with أَ), not *هَلْ لَا …
subtleties: Spoken Arabic often drops هَلْ and uses intonation alone; in writing it is expected.

absent.reason: No separate word: the definite article al- (الْ) is written joined to the noun and is part of the noun forms (DEF cells); before sun letters it assimilates (الثُّومُ).
No indefinite article: an indefinite noun takes nunation (tanwīn: -un, -an, -in); diptotes and indeclinable nouns simply have no article.
